questions.problem:
Find the sum modulo $24$ of the solutions to the congruence $20x≡16\,(\text{mod}\,24).$

*Hint: You may wish to use trial and error to find the appropriate multiplicative inverse.*
questions.worked_solution:
In the given congruence, we have $a=20$ and $n=24$, and so

$$
\text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(20,24)=4.
$$

Since $b=16$ is divisible by $4,$ our congruence has $4$ solutions.

First, we use the division property of congruences:

$$
\begin{aligned}20x & ≡16 &  & (\text{mod}\,24) \\ 4\cdot 5x & ≡4\cdot 4 &  & (\text{mod}\,4\cdot 6) \\ \cancel{4}\cdot 5x & ≡\cancel{4}\cdot 4 &  & (\text{mod}\,\cancel{4}\cdot 6) \\ 5x & ≡4 &  & (\text{mod}\,6)\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in the new congruence, we have ${a}_{1}=5$ and ${n}_{1}=6$, where

$$
\text{gcd}({a}_{1},{n}_{1})=\text{gcd}(5,6)=1.
$$

So, our congruence has a unique solution modulo $6.$

To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $5\,(\text{mod}\,6).$ To find the inverse of $5\,(\text{mod}\,6),$ we compute the exponents of $5\,(\text{mod}\,6)$ until we get a result of $1\,(\text{mod}\,6):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{2} & ≡5\cdot 5≡25≡4\cdot 6+1≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,6)\end{aligned}
$$

So, $5\cdot 5≡1\,(\text{mod}\,6),$ which means that $5$ is its own multiplicative inverse (modulo $6$).

Now, multiplying both sides of our congruence by $5,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}5x & ≡4 &  & (\text{mod}\,6) \\ 5\cdot 5x & ≡5\cdot 4 &  & (\text{mod}\,6) \\ (5\cdot 5)x & ≡20 &  & (\text{mod}\,6) \\ x & ≡20 &  & (\text{mod}\,6) \\ x & ≡3\cdot 6+2 &  & (\text{mod}\,6) \\ x & ≡2 &  & (\text{mod}\,6)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the solution $x≡2\,(\text{mod}\,6).$ 

But our original congruence was modulo $24$ (not modulo $6$). To find all the solutions modulo $24,$ we repeatedly add $6$ modulo $24$ until we reach the number $2$ again:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ≡2 &  & (\text{mod}\,24) \\ {x}_{2} & ≡2+6≡8 &  & (\text{mod}\,24) \\ {x}_{3} & ≡8+6≡14 &  & (\text{mod}\,24) \\ {x}_{4} & ≡14+6≡20 &  & (\text{mod}\,24) \\ {x}_{5} & ≡20+6≡26≡24+2≡2≡{x}_{1} &  & (\text{mod}\,24)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x≡2,8,14,20\,(\text{mod}\,24).$ 

Finally,

$$
2+8+14+20≡44≡24+20≡20\,(\text{mod}\,24).
$$

questions.problem:
Find the sum modulo $33$ of the solutions to the congruence $15x≡18\,(\text{mod}\,33).$

*Hint: You may wish to use trial and error to find the appropriate multiplicative inverse.*
questions.worked_solution:
In the given congruence, we have $a=15$ and $n=33$, and so

$$
\text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(15,33)=3.
$$

Since $b=18$ is divisible by $3,$ our congruence has $3$ solutions.

First, we use the division property of congruences:

$$
\begin{aligned}15x & ≡18 &  & (\text{mod}\,33) \\ 3\cdot 5x & ≡3\cdot 6 &  & (\text{mod}\,3\cdot 11) \\ \cancel{3}\cdot 5x & ≡\cancel{3}\cdot 6 &  & (\text{mod}\,\cancel{3}\cdot 11) \\ 5x & ≡6 &  & (\text{mod}\,11)\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in the new congruence above, we have ${a}_{1}=5$ and ${n}_{1}=11$, where

$$
\text{gcd}({a}_{1},{n}_{1})=\text{gcd}(5,11)=1.
$$

So, our congruence has a unique solution modulo $11.$
To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $5\,(\text{mod}\,11).$ And to find the inverse of $5\,(\text{mod}\,11),$ we compute the exponents of $5\,(\text{mod}\,11)$ until we get a result of $1\,(\text{mod}\,11):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{2} & ≡25≡2\cdot 11+3≡3 &  & (\text{mod}\,11) \\ {5}^{3} & ≡3\cdot 5≡15≡11+4≡4 &  & (\text{mod}\,11) \\ {5}^{4} & ≡4\cdot 5≡20≡11+9≡9 &  & (\text{mod}\,11) \\ {5}^{5} & ≡9\cdot 5≡45≡4\cdot 11+1≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,11)\end{aligned}
$$

So, $9\cdot 5≡1\,(\text{mod}\,11),$ which means that $9$ is the multiplicative inverse of $5$ (modulo $11$).

Now, multiplying both sides of our congruence by $9,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5x & ≡6 &  & (\text{mod}\,11) \\ 9\cdot 5x & ≡9\cdot 6 &  & (\text{mod}\,11) \\ (9\cdot 5)x & ≡54 &  & (\text{mod}\,11) \\ x & ≡54 &  & (\text{mod}\,11) \\ x & ≡4\cdot 11+10 &  & (\text{mod}\,11) \\ x & ≡10 &  & (\text{mod}\,11)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the solution $x≡10\,(\text{mod}\,11).$ 

But our original congruence was modulo $33$ (not modulo $11$). To find all the solutions modulo $33,$ we repeatedly add $11$ modulo $33$ until we reach the number $10$ again:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ≡10 &  & (\text{mod}\,33) \\ {x}_{2} & ≡10+11≡21 &  & (\text{mod}\,33) \\ {x}_{3} & ≡21+11≡32 &  & (\text{mod}\,33) \\ {x}_{4} & ≡32+11≡43≡1\cdot 33+10≡10≡{x}_{1} &  & (\text{mod}\,18)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x≡10,21,32\,(\text{mod}\,33).$ 

Finally,

$$
10+21+32≡63≡33+30≡30\,(\text{mod}\,33).
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following congruences have *precisely four* solutions modulo $24?$

I. $20x≡6\,(\text{mod}\,24)$

II. $16x≡8\,(\text{mod}\,24)$

III. $28x≡8\,(\text{mod}\,24)$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14274573/assets/b65fc4830e0b060d62226b41d5ccb7bdc63d0ad594f7a42a2628597409bba3af.png)

      

Recall the following facts regarding the congruence $ax≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n):$

- The congruence has no solutions modulo $n$ if and only if 

$$
\text{gcd}(a,n)\,\text{⧸}|\,b.
$$

- The congruence has $\text{gcd}(a,n)$ solutions modulo $n$ if and only if 

$$
\text{gcd}(a,n)\,|\,b.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our congruences.

- Congruence I has no solutions. We have $a=20$ and $n=24$, and so

$$
\text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(20,24)=4.
$$

Since $b=6$ is not divisible by $4,$ this congruence has no solutions.

- Congruence II has eight solutions modulo $24.$ We have $a=16$ and $n=24$, and so

$$
\text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(16,24)=8.
$$

Since $b=8$ is divisible by $8,$ this congruence has $8$ solutions.

- Congruence III has four solutions modulo $24.$ We have $a=28$ and $n=24$, and so

$$
\text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(28,24)=4.
$$

Since $b=8$ is divisible by $4,$ this congruence has $4$ solutions.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

questions.worked_solution:
In the given congruence, we have $a=268$ and $n=404$, and we're given that

$$
\text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(268,404)=4.
$$

Since $b=16$ is divisible by $4,$ our congruence has $4$ solutions.

Next, we use the division property of congruences:

$$
\begin{aligned}268x & ≡16 &  & (\text{mod}\,404) \\ 4\cdot 67x & ≡4\cdot 4 &  & (\text{mod}\,4\cdot 101) \\ \cancel{4}\cdot 67x & ≡\cancel{4}\cdot 4 &  & (\text{mod}\,\cancel{4}\cdot 101) \\ 67x & ≡4 &  & (\text{mod}\,101)\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in this new congruence, we have ${a}_{1}=67$ and ${n}_{1}=101$, where

$$
\text{gcd}({a}_{1},{n}_{1})=\text{gcd}(67,101)=1.
$$

So, our congruence has a unique solution modulo $101.$

To find the solution, we must multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $67\,(\text{mod}\,101).$ To find the inverse of $67\,(\text{mod}\,101),$ we apply the extended Euclidean algorithm.

First, we apply the forward reduction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}101 & = & 67\cdot 1 & + & 34\, & ⇔ & \,34 & = & 101-67\cdot 1 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  &  &  \\ 67 & = & 34\cdot 1 & + & 33\, & ⇔ & \,33 & = & 67-34\cdot 1 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  &  &  \\ 34 & = & 33\cdot 1 & + & 1\, & ⇔ & \,1 & = & 34-33\cdot 1 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  &  &  \\ 33 & = & 33\cdot 1 & + & 0\, &  & \, &  & \end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, back-substituting in the usual way gives the following:

$$
1=2\cdot 101-3\cdot 67
$$

We can write this result in modulo $101,$ as follows:  

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot 101-3\cdot 67 & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,101) \\ -3\cdot 67 & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,101) \\ (101-3)\cdot 67 & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,101) \\ 98\cdot 67 & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,101)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse of $67$ modulo $101$ is $98.$

Now, multiplying both sides of our original congruence by $98,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}67x & ≡4 &  & (\text{mod}\,101) \\ 98\cdot 67x & ≡98\cdot 4 &  & (\text{mod}\,101) \\ x & ≡392 &  & (\text{mod}\,101) \\ x & ≡101\cdot 3+89 &  & (\text{mod}\,101) \\ x & ≡89 &  & (\text{mod}\,101)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the solution $x≡89\,(\text{mod}\,101).$

But our original congruence was modulo $404$ (not modulo $101$). To find all the solutions modulo $404,$ we repeatedly add $101$ to $89$ modulo $404$ until we reach the number $89$ again:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ≡89 &  & (\text{mod}\,404) \\ {x}_{2} & ≡89+101≡190 &  & (\text{mod}\,404) \\ {x}_{3} & ≡190+101≡291 &  & (\text{mod}\,404) \\ {x}_{4} & ≡291+101≡392 &  & (\text{mod}\,404) \\ {x}_{5} & ≡392+101≡493≡404+89≡{x}_{1} &  & (\text{mod}\,404)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are 

$$
{x}_{1,2,3,4}≡89,\,190,\,291,\,392\,(\text{mod}\,404).
$$

In the given congruence, we have $a=92$ and $n=284$, and we're given that

$$
\text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(92,284)=4.
$$

Since $b=24$ is divisible by $4,$ our congruence has $4$ solutions.

Next, we use the division property of congruences:

$$
\begin{aligned}92x & ≡24 &  & (\text{mod}\,284) \\ 4\cdot 23x & ≡4\cdot 6 &  & (\text{mod}\,4\cdot 71) \\ \cancel{4}\cdot 23x & ≡\cancel{4}\cdot 6 &  & (\text{mod}\,\cancel{4}\cdot 71) \\ 23x & ≡6 &  & (\text{mod}\,71)\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in this new congruence, we have ${a}_{1}=23$ and ${n}_{1}=71$, where

$$
\text{gcd}({a}_{1},{n}_{1})=\text{gcd}(23,71)=1.
$$

So, our congruence has a unique solution modulo $71.$

To find the solution, we must multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $23\,(\text{mod}\,71).$ To find the inverse of $23\,(\text{mod}\,71),$ we apply the extended Euclidean algorithm.

First, we apply the forward reduction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}71 & = & 23\cdot 3 & + & 2\, & ⇔ & \,2 & = & 71-23\cdot 3 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  &  &  \\ 23 & = & 11\cdot 2 & + & 1\, & ⇔ & \,1 & = & 23-11\cdot 2 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  &  &  \\ 11 & = & 11\cdot 1 & + & 0\, &  & \, &  & \end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, back-substituting in the usual way gives the following:

$$
1=34\cdot 23-11\cdot 71
$$

We can write this result in modulo $71,$ as follows:  

$$
\begin{aligned}34\cdot 23-11\cdot 71 & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,71) \\ 34\cdot 23 & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,71)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse of $23$ modulo $71$ is $34.$

Now, multiplying both sides of our original congruence by $34,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}23x & ≡6 &  & (\text{mod}\,71) \\ 34\cdot 23x & ≡34\cdot 6 &  & (\text{mod}\,71) \\ x & ≡204 &  & (\text{mod}\,71) \\ x & ≡71\cdot 2+62 &  & (\text{mod}\,71) \\ x & ≡62 &  & (\text{mod}\,71)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the solution $x≡62\,(\text{mod}\,71).$

But our original congruence was modulo $284$ (not modulo $71$). To find all the solutions modulo $284,$ we repeatedly add $71$ to $62$ modulo $284$ until we reach the number $62$ again:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ≡62 &  & (\text{mod}\,284) \\ {x}_{2} & ≡62+71≡133 &  & (\text{mod}\,284) \\ {x}_{3} & ≡133+71≡204 &  & (\text{mod}\,284) \\ {x}_{4} & ≡204+71≡275 &  & (\text{mod}\,284) \\ {x}_{5} & ≡275+71≡346≡284+62≡{x}_{1} &  & (\text{mod}\,284)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are 

$$
{x}_{1,2,3,4}≡62,\,133,\,204,\,275\,(\text{mod}\,284).
$$
